quotes.text: Since their sophomore album, Discovery, the human/robot dichotomy and its relationship with that lovin' feeling have been a part of Daft Punk's narrative.

After 1997's Homework, which drew heavily from Chicago house, Daft Punk took a baby step in the direction they would take over a decade later for Random Access Memories, and Discovery was decidedly warmer and more emotional than their debut.
It's no coincidence that both songs humanize the dancefloor, giving back life (and love) to the dead-eyed ravers jacking to the beat, trying to get some before the sun comes up.

Daft Punk went there for their new album partially in reaction to contemporary electronic music. In their recent cover story interview with Rolling Stone, Bangalter said, "Today, electronic music is like an audio energy drink. Artists are overcompensating with this aggressive, energetic, hyperstimulating music — it's like someone shaking you. But it can't move people on an emotional level."

Many of the voices on Random Access Memories are laden with effects, and Daft Punk have admitted they couldn't have made this record without computers, but this time they put that digital love into production value.

This is an album made for courtship and seduction, not sex behind the speakers. Daft Punk did, as they set out to do, outpace their successors and fans who then accused them, somewhat unfairly, of abandoning their "original sound" as of nearly 15 years ago.
The reality is that Daft Punk have been reinventing themselves even before they were Daft Punk.
His song, "Touch," might be the album's most powerful statement of the new Daft Punk, indicative of their evolution.
Made in six weeks, paced to work alongside Electroma, and supposedly the result of "pure improvisation," the album comes off cheap and erratic even to the untrained ear.

On this song, Daft Punk took the chorus to heart and made their dreams come true, playing the same Wurlitzer that Supertramp used on a bridge that was supposed to sound like the '70s prog-rock titans themselves stepped in to noodle around.

O'Sullivan wrote and produced "Alone Again (Naturally)" himself. He's insisted that it wasn't autobiographical. His mother was still alive when the song came out. His father had died when O'Sullivan was 11, and O'Sullivan hadn't known him well. Maybe that's why O'Sullivan doesn't sound even remotely broken when he's singing about being broken. He's singing about heartbreak -- not from lived experience, but from coming up with the saddest, most melodramatic situations that he can imagine.

Musically, though, it's an amiable and low-key amble, all fluttery acoustic guitars and woodwind tootles and soft string-swirls. It's dentist's-office music. And O'Sullivan never reaches out for any big notes. He just plainly presents his absurdly depressing scenarios with a forthright, conversational plainness.

Much has been made of the polarized songwriters at the center of Supertramp's best music. Without Rick Davies and Roger Hodgson's contrasting styles and their shared commitment to the band's albums, Supertramp's history could have turned out quite different.
Once unsaddled and more focused, a reliable lineup was in place, and the records began to envelop the sounds of pop and art-rock alongside the still-present progressive music.

once the group — along with Davies and Hodgson, saxophonist John Helliwell, bassist Dougie Thomson and drummer Bob Siebenberg — found its stride with 1974's Crime of the Century, it was a determined and inevitable climb to Breakfast in America, the multiplatinum No. 1 that made Supertramp one of the world's biggest bands at the end of the decade.
Their 11 albums tell the story, from ambitious prog hopefuls to America-conquering superstars.
